summary: This Standards Track document gives compliance statements for the CMC enrollment protocol, the information needed to build a compliant implementation. The ASN.1 and transports are covered in RFC 10002 and RFC 10003. It obsoletes RFC 5274 and RFC 6402.

plainLanguage.summary: CMC is the protocol a program uses to ask a certificate authority to issue a certificate. This document is the checklist for anyone writing that program: which encryption algorithms are acceptable, which optional features each kind of participant has to support, and what a certificate authority must check before it signs. It does not define the protocol itself, only what counts as a conformant implementation of it.

questions: which controls must a cmc ca support
what algorithms must cmc entities support
subtitle: The rules a Certificate Management over CMS implementation has to follow to be conformant.

tldr.problem: The Certificate Management over CMS protocol has been written across several documents, so an implementer had no single place that said which algorithms and which features were actually required.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists the algorithms every party must support and a table giving, for each control of the protocol, the level of support required from end entities, registration authorities and certification authorities.
tldr.outcome: This obsoletes RFC 5274 and RFC 6402. It moves the hash from SHA-1 to SHA-256, adds the authenticated encryption algorithms, and states the requirements once, in one table.

today: RFC 10004 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current compliance statement for the CMC enrollment protocol. It obsoleted RFC 5274 and RFC 6402, and it sits alongside RFC 10002, which defines the CMC structures, and RFC 10003, which defines its transports.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
The Certificate Management over CMS protocol is designed in terms of a client/server relationship. In the simplest case, the client is the requestor of the certificate, the End-Entity, and the server is the issuer of the certificate, the Certification Authority. The introduction of a Registration Authority into the set of agents complicates the picture only slightly. The RA becomes the server with respect to the certificate requestor, and it becomes the client with respect to the certificate issuer. Any number of RAs can be inserted into the picture in this manner.

The RAs may serve specialized purposes that are not currently covered by this document. One such purpose would be a Key Escrow agent, in which case all certificate requests for encryption keys would be directed through this RA and it would take appropriate action to do the key archival. Key recovery requests could be defined in the CMC methodology, allowing for the Key Escrow agent to perform that operation as the final server in the chain of agents.

If there are multiple RAs in the system, it is considered normal that not all RAs will see all certificate requests. The routing between the RAs may be dependent on the content of the certificate requests involved.

The document is divided into sections specifying the requirements that are specific to a class of agents in the CMC model: all entities, all servers, all clients, all EEs, all RAs and all CAs. The ASN.1 structures and the transport mechanisms for the CMC enrollment protocol are covered in other documents, RFC 10002 and RFC 10003.
sections.plainLanguage: CMC is a client and server protocol. The party that wants a certificate asks for it, and the party that signs certificates answers. A registration authority can sit in between, so that the certificate authority does not have to talk to every applicant directly. This document says what each of those parties must do.

sections.title: The Roles in the CMC Model
sections.content:
The End-Entity is the entity that owns a key pair and for whom a certificate is issued. A Registration Authority, also called a Local RA, is an entity that acts as an intermediary between the EE and the CA. Multiple RAs can exist between the EE and the CA, and RAs may perform additional services such as key generation or key archival. The document uses the term RA for both.

The Certification Authority is the entity that issues certificates. A Client is an entity that creates a Public Key Infrastructure Request; both RAs and EEs can be clients. A Server is an entity that processes PKI Requests and creates PKI Responses; both CAs and RAs can be servers.

PKCS #10 refers to the Public Key Cryptography Standard #10, which defines a certification request syntax. CRMF refers to the Certificate Request Message Format, which CMC uses as part of the protocol. CMS refers to the Cryptographic Message Syntax, and the document provides for basic cryptographic services including encryption and signing with and without key management.

PKI Requests include certification requests and revocation requests; PKI Responses include certs-only messages and failure messages. Proof-of-Identity refers to the client proving they are who they say they are to the server. Proof-of-Possession refers to a value that can be used to prove that the private key corresponding to a public key is in the possession and can be used by an EE. The transport wrapper is the outermost CMS wrapping layer, and an entity means an EE, RA or CA.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names four roles: the applicant that owns the key, the registration authority that checks the applicant, the certificate authority that signs, and the chain that connects them. Two ideas run through it: proving who you are, and proving that you really hold the private key that matches the public key in the certificate.

sections.title: What Changed Since RFCs 5274 and 6402
sections.content:
The document merges the text of the CMC Updates document, RFC 6402. It updated the Introduction, changed the phrase all agents to all entities in the overview to maintain consistency throughout the document, and renumbered the section headers.

It added the RA Identity Proof Witness and Response Body controls to the control table. It updated the Cryptographic Algorithm Requirements: SHA-1 was replaced with SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-1 was replaced with HMAC-SHA-256, and algorithms for AuthEnvelopedData were added. A paragraph was added to maintain backward algorithm compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The older hash algorithm has been retired in favour of SHA-256 and its message authentication code. Two controls were added to the table, and a rule was added so that older algorithms may still be offered on request while the stronger ones are used by default.

sections.title: Requirements for All Entities
sections.content:
All compliance statements of the CMC structure and transport documents MUST be adhered to unless specifically stated otherwise in this document.

All entities MUST support Full PKI Requests, Simple PKI Responses and Full PKI Responses. Servers SHOULD support Simple PKI Requests. All entities MUST support the use of the CRMF syntax for certification requests, while support for the PKCS #10 syntax for certification requests SHOULD be implemented by servers.

The extendedFailInfo field SHOULD NOT be populated in the CMCStatusInfoV2 object; the failInfo field SHOULD be used to relay this information. If the extendedFailInfo field is used, it is suggested that an additional CMCStatusInfoV2 item exist for the same body part with a failInfo field.

All entities MUST implement the HTTP transport mechanism as defined in the CMC transport document. Other transport mechanisms MAY be implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: Every participant has to be able to send the fuller kind of request and both kinds of answer, and to read the certificate request format the protocol uses. On top of that, everyone has to offer the HTTP transport, and may offer others as well.

sections.title: Cryptographic Algorithm Requirements
sections.content:
All entities MUST verify RSA-SHA256 signatures in SignedData and MUST generate RSA-SHA256 signatures for SignedData. Entities MAY verify and generate other signature algorithms. All entities MUST support the Advanced Encryption Standard as the content encryption algorithm for EnvelopedData, and other content encryption algorithms MAY be implemented.

All entities MUST support AES-GCM, Galois/Counter Mode, as the authenticated content encryption algorithm for AuthEnvelopedData. They MUST also support a 12-octet nonce size and a 12-octet Integrity Check Value length. All entities MUST support RSA as a key transport algorithm for EnvelopedData and AuthEnvelopedData. If an entity supports key agreement for EnvelopedData or AuthEnvelopedData, it MUST support Diffie-Hellman.

If an entity supports PasswordRecipientInfo for EnvelopedData, AuthenticatedData or AuthEnvelopedData, it MUST support the Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2 for key derivation algorithms and MUST support AES key wrap as the key encryption algorithm. If AuthenticatedData is supported, PasswordRecipientInfo MUST be supported.

The algorithm requirements for the Identity Proof Version 2 control are that SHA-256 MUST be implemented for hashAlgId and HMAC-SHA256 MUST be implemented for macAlgId. For the Pop Link Witness Version 2 control, SHA-256 MUST be implemented for keyGenAlgorithm, PBKDF2 MAY be implemented for keyGenAlgorithm, and HMAC-SHA256 MUST be implemented for macAlgorithm. For the Encrypted POP and Decrypted POP controls, SHA-256 MUST be implemented for witnessAlgID and HMAC-SHA256 MUST be implemented for thePOPAlgID. For the Publish Trust Anchors control, SHA-256 MUST be implemented for hashAlgorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm choices are fixed rather than open. Signing uses RSA with SHA-256. Ordinary encrypted messages use AES, and messages that also carry their own integrity check use AES-GCM with a 12-octet nonce and a 12-octet check value. Where a key is agreed with Diffie-Hellman, that is the required method.

sections.title: Which Controls Each Role Must Support
sections.content:
The document gives a table listing the name and level of support required for each control, with a column for each of the End-Entity, the RA and the CA. The controls required of every role are Extended CMC Status Info, Identity Proof Version 2, Identification, POP Link Random, POP Link Witness Version 2, Data Return, Transaction ID, Sender Nonce, Recipient Nonce, Query Pending and Confirm Cert. Acceptance, all at level MUST. CMC Status Info, Identity Proof, POP Link Witness, Registration Info and Response Information are at level SHOULD for every role.

Some controls do not apply to every role. Modify Cert Request, Batch Request, Batch Responses, Control Processed and RA Identity Proof Witness are marked N/A for the End-Entity and MUST for the RA, while the CA entry for each of them is marked as a note: the CA MUST implement the control if designed to work with RAs. Revocation Request is SHOULD for the EE and the RA and MUST for the CA. Get Certificate, Get CRL and Publication Information are OPTIONAL for every role.

Encrypted POP and Decrypted POP have notes: EEs only need to implement them if they support key agreement algorithms, or if they need to operate in environments where the hardware keys cannot provide POP, and RAs SHOULD implement them if they implement RA POP Witness. Publish Trust Anchors and Authenticated Data are OPTIONAL for every role, but the document says strong consideration should be given to implementing them, because this gives a simple method for distributing trust anchors to clients without user intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is the heart of the document. Each optional piece of the protocol is listed, with the level each kind of participant must reach. Some pieces only make sense for a registration authority, and the certificate authority only needs them if it works with registration authorities.

sections.title: Requirements for Certification Authorities
sections.content:
Providing for CAs to work in an environment with RAs is strongly suggested, because this permits the delegation of substantial administrative interaction onto an RA rather than at the CA.

CAs MUST perform at least minimal checks on all public keys before issuing a certificate. At a minimum, a check for syntax would occur with the POP operation. Additionally, CAs SHOULD perform simple checks for known bad keys such as small subgroups for DSA-SHA1 and DH keys, or known bad exponents for RSA keys.

CAs MUST enforce POP checking before issuing any certificate. CAs MAY delegate the POP operation to an RA for those cases where a challenge and response message pair must be used, where an RA performs escrow of a key and checks for POP in that manner, or where an unusual algorithm is used and that validation is done at the RA. CAs SHOULD implement both the DH-POP Proof-of-Possession and the challenge-response POP controls id-cmc-encryptedPOP and id-cmc-decryptedPOP.

There are no additional requirements for clients or for servers. If an EE implements Diffie-Hellman, it MUST implement either the DH POP Proof-of-Possession or the challenge-response POP controls. RAs SHOULD be able to do delegated POP, and an RA implementing that feature MUST implement the id-cmc-lraPOPWitness control. All RAs MUST implement the promotion of the id-aa-cmc-unsignedData.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate authority is the one that must be careful. Before it signs anything it has to check that the applicant really holds the matching private key, and it should also screen the key itself for known weaknesses. It may hand that check to a registration authority in some cases, but it stays responsible for the outcome.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document uses the CMC structure and transport documents as building blocks, and the security sections of those two documents are included by reference.

Knowledge of how an entity is expected to operate is vital in determining which sections of requirements are applicable to that entity. Care needs to be taken in determining which sections apply and fully implementing the necessary code.

Cryptographic algorithms have and will be broken or weakened. Implementers and users need to check that the cryptographic algorithms listed in this document make sense from a security level. The IETF from time to time may issue documents dealing with the current state of the art, and two examples of such documents are the small-subgroup attacks paper and the attacks on cryptographic hashes paper.
sections.plainLanguage: The security reasoning is inherited from the two documents that define the protocol itself. This document adds one warning: the algorithms named here will one day be too weak, so an implementation has to be able to change them.

messages.label: PKI REQUEST
messages.note: The end-entity asks for a certificate. The RA is the server here.

messages.label: PKI REQUEST
messages.note: The RA is a client towards the CA, which issues the certificate.

messages.label: PKI RESPONSE
messages.note: The certificate comes back down the chain.

items.title: CRMF syntax
items.text: All entities MUST support it for certification requests.

items.title: PKCS #10 syntax
items.text: Servers SHOULD implement it for certification requests.

items.title: HTTP transport
items.text: All entities MUST implement it; other transports MAY be implemented.

viz.caption: THE ALGORITHMS EVERY ENTITY MUST HANDLE

items.label: SignedData signature
items.desc: All entities MUST verify and MUST generate RSA-SHA256 signatures.

items.label: EnvelopedData content encryption
items.desc: All entities MUST support AES as the content encryption algorithm for EnvelopedData.

items.label: AuthEnvelopedData content encryption
items.desc: All entities MUST support AES-GCM, with a 12-octet nonce size and a 12-octet Integrity Check Value length.

items.label: Key transport
items.desc: All entities MUST support RSA as a key transport algorithm for EnvelopedData and AuthEnvelopedData.

items.label: Key agreement
items.desc: If an entity supports key agreement, it MUST support Diffie-Hellman.

items.label: Password-based key derivation
items.desc: Required when PasswordRecipientInfo is supported, together with AES key wrap.

items.label: Hash algorithm
items.desc: SHA-256 MUST be implemented for hashAlgId, keyGenAlgorithm, witnessAlgID and hashAlgorithm.

items.label: MAC algorithm
items.desc: HMAC-SHA256 MUST be implemented for macAlgId, macAlgorithm and thePOPAlgID.
